slides.title: Word2Vec: word vectors from prediction
slides.body:
**Mikolov 2013**: word embeddings as a byproduct of predicting context.

Two variants:
- **Skip-gram**: given target word $w_t$, predict context words $w_{t-k}, \dots, w_{t+k}$.
$$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{-k \le j \le k, j \ne 0} \log P(w_{t+j} \mid w_t)$$
- **CBOW (Continuous Bag-of-Words)**: given context $w_{t-k}, \dots, w_{t+k}$, predict target $w_t$.

Each word has TWO vectors: input embedding $\mathbf{v}_w$ + output embedding $\mathbf{u}_w$.
$$P(w_o \mid w_i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_{w_o}^T \mathbf{v}_{w_i})}{\sum_{w \in V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^T \mathbf{v}_{w_i})}$$

In practice, only $\mathbf{v}$ (input embedding) is used downstream.

**The bottleneck**: the softmax over $V$ (often 100K+) is expensive per update. Two practical fixes:
- **Hierarchical softmax**: tree-structured softmax over vocabulary, $O(\log V)$.
- **Negative sampling**: turn the softmax into a binary classification (positive context vs $k$ random negatives). Trains much faster.

Negative sampling won — it's THE standard implementation. With $k = 5$ negatives, training is ~100× faster than full softmax for vocab $V = 100K$.

**The geometry**:
- Words appearing in similar contexts get similar embeddings (high cosine similarity).
- Linear-analogy: famously, $\mathbf{v}_{king} - \mathbf{v}_{man} + \mathbf{v}_{woman} \approx \mathbf{v}_{queen}$.
- Captured semantics: dog/cat/fish cluster (animals); Monday/Tuesday/Wednesday cluster (days).

slides.title: GloVe: factoring the co-occurrence matrix
slides.body:
**GloVe** (Pennington 2014): word embeddings from log-co-occurrence factorization.

Let $X_{ij}$ = count of word $j$ in word $i$'s context. Define:
$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i, j} f(X_{ij}) (\mathbf{w}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{w}}_j + b_i + \tilde{b}_j - \log X_{ij})^2$$
where $f$ is a weighting function (down-weights both very rare + very frequent pairs).

Train to MAKE $\mathbf{w}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{w}}_j$ approximate $\log X_{ij}$. The dot product captures log-co-occurrence.

**Closed-form-ish flavor**: matrix factorization framing makes GloVe feel more analytical than Word2Vec's stochastic objective. Empirically they give similar-quality vectors.

**Differences**:
- Word2Vec is online (SGD, one example at a time).
- GloVe needs the full co-occurrence matrix in memory (or chunked).
- Quality: roughly equivalent on most benchmarks.

**fastText** (Bojanowski 2017): extend Word2Vec with subword n-grams. Each word's embedding = sum of its character-n-gram embeddings. Handles OOV: a new word's embedding = sum of its known character-n-grams. Critical for morphologically-rich languages.

**These three** (Word2Vec, GloVe, fastText) defined the 'static embedding' era 2013-2018. Every NLP pipeline used pretrained word vectors as initialization. Replaced by contextual embeddings (next slide).

slides.title: Contextual embeddings: ELMo → BERT → GPT
slides.body:
**The problem with static embeddings**: 'bank' has ONE vector — whether the context is finance or rivers. Polysemy hurts.

**ELMo** (Peters 2018): contextual word embeddings from a deep bidirectional LSTM trained as a language model. Each word's embedding is a function of the full sentence.

ELMo's training:
- Forward LM: predict $w_t$ given $w_1, \dots, w_{t-1}$.
- Backward LM: predict $w_t$ given $w_{t+1}, \dots, w_T$.
- Concatenate forward + backward representations at each layer.
- Downstream: weighted sum of the layers' representations.

**BERT** (Devlin 2018): the seminal transformer-based contextual model.
- **Masked LM (MLM)**: randomly mask 15% of tokens; predict them from context. The model sees BOTH sides bidirectionally in one pass (vs ELMo's separate forward + backward LSTMs).
- **Next-sentence prediction (NSP)**: predict if sentence B follows sentence A. (Later shown to be optional.)
- Pretrained on BooksCorpus + Wikipedia. Fine-tune on downstream tasks.

**Results**: BERT shattered every NLP benchmark in late 2018. GLUE went from ~70% (pre-BERT SOTAs) to ~83% (BERT-base) to ~89% (RoBERTa, BERT-large with more data). The pretraining + fine-tuning paradigm was unlocked.

**GPT** (2018-19): same idea, but causal/decoder-only. Predict each token from the left context. Scales to massive sizes (GPT-3: 175B parameters). Few-shot in-context learning emerges at scale.

**Modern**: encoder-only (BERT family) for classification / extraction / similarity. Decoder-only (GPT family) for generation + the dominant LLM line. Encoder-decoder (T5, BART) for translation + summarization.

**Embedding-only use cases**: even today, sentence-BERT / E5 / BGE etc. produce a single embedding vector per document for retrieval (RAG). These are contextual (the whole document is embedded as one vector based on its content).

question.question: Derive the Word2Vec skip-gram gradient
question.goal: Skip-gram with negative sampling. Loss for a single (target=$w_i$, context=$w_o$) positive pair + $k$ negatives $w_{n_1}, \dots, w_{n_k}$: $\mathcal{L} = -\log\sigma(\mathbf{u}_{w_o}^T \mathbf{v}_{w_i}) - \sum_{j=1}^k \log\sigma(-\mathbf{u}_{w_{n_j}}^T \mathbf{v}_{w_i})$.

hints: $\sigma(x) - 1 = -\sigma(-x)$. And the negative outside flips sign.
steps.reveal: Gradient: $(\sigma(\mathbf{u}_{w_o}^T \mathbf{v}_{w_i}) - 1) \mathbf{v}_{w_i}$. Move $\mathbf{u}_{w_o}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{v}_{w_i}$ (positive scale: pull together).

steps.prompt: Update rule (SGD with lr $\eta$): $\mathbf{u}_{w_o} \leftarrow \mathbf{u}_{w_o} - \eta \cdot \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \mathbf{u}_{w_o}$. Interpret in plain English what happens to $\mathbf{u}_{w_o}$ during one positive-pair update.

options: $\mathbf{u}_{w_o}$ moves TOWARD $\mathbf{v}_{w_i}$ (since $\sigma < 1$, the coefficient is negative + the SGD step subtracts a negative).

hints: Coefficient $\sigma - 1 < 0$. SGD subtracts gradient → $u$ moves towards $v$.
steps.reveal: Positive pair pulls $\mathbf{u}_{w_o}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{w_i}$ together. Negative pairs push apart. Word vectors organize by co-occurrence.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{SGD pulls together co-occurring word vectors, pushes apart sampled negatives}}$$ The simple gradient updates produce the famous semantic geometry. Words appearing in similar contexts have their input + output vectors pulled together (transitively, through shared contexts). The negative-sampling efficiency made Word2Vec practical at billion-token scale. The same gradient pattern underlies every contrastive learning algorithm in modern ML (SimCLR, CLIP, etc.).

question.question: The famous Word2Vec analogy 'king − man + woman ≈ queen' works because:
options: The model was trained on royalty-specific data.

The training objective (predicting context) makes semantic-similarity dimensions ALIGN linearly in the embedding space — co-occurrence patterns of 'king/queen' share regions, with the 'man/woman' direction crossing them.
question.explanation: Distributional patterns of 'king' + 'queen' overlap heavily (both monarchs, royal contexts). Their difference (along the 'gender' direction) is approximately parallel to 'man - woman'. So king + (woman - man) lands near queen. This is an EMERGENT geometric property — not designed. It's also LIMITED: analogies work cleanly on a few dimensions (gender, capital-of-country) but fail on most.

slides.workedSolution: Word2Vec / GloVe produce embeddings where semantic dimensions (gender, country-capital, plural-of, verb-tense) correspond to ROUGHLY linear directions. Pulled out by SVD on the embedding matrix. The analogy `a - b + c` walks in the analogous direction. It's emergent from contextual statistics — words sharing the relation also share co-occurrence patterns. Works imperfectly: ~70% accuracy on the standard analogy benchmarks for gender + nationality; much lower for harder relations.

Embeddings for semantic search
question.prompt: Your team builds a Q&A retrieval system. Word2Vec embeddings give poor results compared to BERT-based sentence embeddings. Walk through why.
Explain in two or three sentences why contextual embeddings (BERT, ELMo) replaced static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) for most NLP tasks.
question.rubric: Mentions that static embeddings give one vector per word regardless of context (failing for polysemous words like 'bank'); contextual embeddings produce a different vector each time based on surrounding sentence; this resolves polysemy + captures fine-grained meaning. Pretrained transformer encoders also serve as transfer-learning bases, making them the foundation of modern NLP pipelines.
